### Distortion Analysis: PT-Heavy vs FT-Skewed

**Part-time-heavy models (Walmart, Target, TJX, Dollar General):**
- Walmart: ~60–65% part-time. Reported headcount of 2.1M greatly overstates labor inputs vs. FTE equivalent of ~900,000 FTEs. Revenue/employee ($309k) understates true productivity by ~40%.
- Target: ~50–55% part-time. Estimated FTE ~220,000, implying FTE revenue = ~$485k.
- Dollar General: >60% part-time given 8–10 employees per store. Revenue/employee is misleadingly low; per-store revenue ~$2.2M at 20,594 stores.
- TJX: Treasure-hunt model relies on rapid replenishment; ~50% PT. Revenue/FTE likely ~$225k vs $155k per head.

**Full-time-skewed models (Costco, Aldi Süd):**
- Costco: ~75% FT (by company disclosure of ~$25+/hr average wages, benefits); 333,000 workers in 891 warehouses = 374 workers/warehouse. Revenue/employee $764k — highest among public entities — reflects FT efficiency and high per-warehouse throughput (~$275M revenue/warehouse).
- Aldi Süd: Approximately 8–12 employees per store (very lean model); estimated 150,000–200,000 global employees; mostly full-time given operational demands. Revenue/FTE adjustment magnitude: minimal (already largely FT).

**FTE Adjustment Magnitude:**
- Walmart: Adjusting for PT ratio, FTE-equivalent revenue jumps from $309k → ~$440k (+42% upward revision)
- Target: $237k → ~$400k (+69%)
- Dollar General: $218k → ~$330k (+51%)
- Costco: $764k → ~$900k (+18%) — much smaller because already FT-heavy

- **Dollar General, Pepco, Aldi Süd, and Action** have negligible digital — these are convenience/discount models where the customer mission is immediate need/high-frequency fill-in trips.

## Q6. Labor Productivity — Revenue per Employee and FTE Adjustment

| Entity | Total Revenue ($B) | Employees (headcount) | FTE Reported | Revenue/Employee ($K) | Revenue/FTE ($K) | Stores | Stores per 1,000 Employees | Labor Model |
|--------|------------------|---------------------|-------------|---------------------|-----------------|-------|--------------------------|------------|
| **Walmart** | $681.0 | 2,100,000 | ~1,470,000* (est. 70% FTE) | $324 | ~$463 | 10,771 | 5.1 | Part-time heavy |
| **Costco** | $254.5 | 333,000 | ~310,000* (est. 93% FTE) | $764 | ~$821 | 891 | 2.7 | Full-time skewed |
| **Target** | $106.6 | 415,000 | ~315,000* (est. 76% FTE) | $257 | ~$338 | 1,978 | 4.8 | Part-time heavy |
| **Dollar General** | $40.6 | 185,800 | ~120,000* (est. 65% FTE) | $219 | ~$338 | 20,594 | 110.8 | Ultra-lean store staffing |
| **TJX** | $56.4 | 364,000 | ~255,000* (est. 70% FTE) | $155 | ~$221 | 5,085 | 14.0 | Part-time retail |
| **Pepco Group** | €6.2B ($6.9B) | ~31,500 | — | ~$220 | — | 4,948 | 157.1 | Lean staffing |
| **Aldi Süd** | €89B ($92.6B) | 203,146 | >90% FTE est. | ~$456 | ~$500 | ~7,955 | 39.2 | Full-time skewed |
| **Action** | €13.8B ($14.4B) | 79,681 | — | ~$181 | — | 2,918 | 36.6 | Lean staffing |

*FTE estimates based on industry disclosures where exact FTE not reported

**Key insights:**
- **Costco** has the highest revenue per employee ($764K) among US-listed entities — its warehouse model with full-time-skewed employment and high membership-driven sales per employee drives this.
- **Walmart** ($324K/employee) appears low but the part-time mix (est. 70% FTE) means revenue/FTE of ~$463K is much closer to Costco on a normalized basis.
- **Dollar General** has extremely low revenue per employee ($219K) but incredibly high stores-per-1,000-employees (110.8) — reflecting its ultra-lean model of ~3-4 employees per store. This is the highest density ratio.
- **Pepco Group** similarly has high store density (157.1 stores per 1,000 employees) due to lean staffing in discount variety.
- **TJX** has the lowest revenue per employee ($155K) — off-price retail requires significant store-level labor for the treasure-hunt model (merchandise handling, frequent replenishment).

**Distortion caused by part-time models:**
- Walmart: Headcount-based metric understates true productivity by ~30% vs FTE
- Target: ~24% understatement vs FTE
- Costco: Only ~7% understatement — near-full-time model
- Aldi Süd: Hard-discount model with mostly full-time, specialized employees; higher revenue/employee than mass merchants

**Sources:**
- Walmart employee count ~2.1M — [Walmart Corporate](https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2025/04/24/walmart-releases-2025-annual-report-and-proxy-statement)
- Costco employee data — [Costco 10-K FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/909832/000090983224000049/cost-20240901.htm)
- Target: 415K employees — [Trading Economics](https://tradingeconomics.com/dg:us:employees)
- Dollar General: 185,800 — [Macrotrends](https://www.macrotrends.net/stocks/charts/DG/dollar-general/number-of-employees)
- TJX: 364,000 — [TJX 10-K FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/109198/000010919825000010/tjx-20250201.htm)
- Pepco: ~31,500 — [Pepco Group](https://www.pepcogroup.eu/our-brands/)
- Aldi Süd: 203,146 — [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldi)
- Action: 79,681 — [Action Press Release](https://company.action.com/pressreleases/action-2024-net-sales-grow-21-7-to-e13-8-billion-like-for-like-growth-10-3/)

## Q7. Per-Store Enterprise Value — Implied Premium by Model

| Entity | Market Cap ($B) | Total Debt ($B) | Cash ($B) | Enterprise Value ($B) | Revenue ($B) | EV/Revenue | Stores | EV/Store ($M) | Model Bucket |
|--------|---------------|---------------|-----------|---------------------|------------|----------|-------|-------------|-------------|
| **Walmart** | ~$670 | ~$52 | ~$11 | ~$711 | $681.0 | 1.04x | 10,771 | $66.0 | Mass Merchant |
| **Costco** | ~$410 | ~$6 | ~$10 | ~$406 | $254.5 | 1.60x | 891 | $455.7 | Warehouse Club |
| **Target** | ~$70 | ~$16 | ~$5 | ~$81 | $106.6 | 0.76x | 1,978 | $41.0 | Mass Merchant |
| **Dollar General** | ~$26 | ~$8 | ~$0.3 | ~$33.7 | $40.6 | 0.83x | 20,594 | $1.6 | Dollar/Hard Discount |
| **TJX** | ~$137 | ~$3 | ~$6 | ~$134 | $56.4 | 2.38x | 5,085 | $26.4 | Off-Price |
| **Pepco Group** | ~$5.1 | ~$0.3** | ~$0.1 | ~$5.3 | $6.9 | 0.77x | 4,948 | $1.1 | Dollar/Hard Discount |
| **Aldi Süd** | ~$80B* (est.) | Minimal | N/A | ~$80B* | $92.6 | ~0.86x | ~7,955 | ~$10.1 | Dollar/Hard Discount |
| **Action** | ~$27B* (3i stake) | ~$2B | ~$0.5 | ~$28.5 | $14.4 | 1.98x | 2,918 | $9.8 | Dollar/Hard Discount |

*Private entity valuations: Aldi Süd estimated from comparable multiples (Aldi Group combined ~€120B+). Action valuation based on 3i's 65.3% stake valued at ~£15.5B implying total EV ~€27B.
**Pepco net debt pre-IFRS 16: €256M = ~$0.3B

**Model Bucket Medians:**

| Bucket | Entities | Median EV/Store ($M) |
|--------|---------|-------------------|
| **Mass Merchant** | Walmart, Target | $53.5 |
| **Warehouse Club** | Costco | $455.7 |
| **Dollar/Hard Discount** | Dollar General, Pepco, Aldi Süd, Action | $5.9 |
| **Off-Price** | TJX | $26.4 |

**Outlier Analysis:**

The single entity that deviates most from its bucket median is **Costco** in the Warehouse Club bucket. Its EV/Store of $455.7M dramatically exceeds all other buckets and reflects:

1. **Membership fee capitalization**: ~65% of operating profit comes from membership fees, creating a subscription-like revenue stream that the market values at a premium (EV/Revenue 1.60x — highest among the top-4 US retailers listed).
2. **Store economics**: Costco warehouses generate ~$280M+ in revenue per unit vs. ~$63M for Walmart US stores — 4.4x higher.
3. **Real estate ownership**: Costco owns most of its warehouses, creating significant asset backing.

Within the Dollar/Hard Discount bucket, **Action** ($9.8M EV/store) is the highest, nearly 6x the bucket median of $1.6M (Dollar General), reflecting Action's 21.7% revenue growth, 10.3% LFL, and 15% EBITDA margins — a clear premium for high-growth, high-return hard discount.

**Sources:**
- Market caps from public data (approximate as of mid-2025)
- Debt/cash from latest 10-Ks (Walmart, Costco, Target, DG, TJX)
- Pepco Group market cap — [CompaniesMarketCap](https://companiesmarketcap.com/pepco-group/marketcap/)
- 3i Group Action valuation — [3i Group AR24](https://www.3i-usinvestors.com/media/nnrkjwke/annual_report_and_accounts_2024.pdf)
- Action stores: 2,918 — [Action](https://company.action.com/pressreleases/action-2024-net-sales-grow-21-7-to-e13-8-billion-like-for-like-growth-10-3/)

---

## Q8. Total Shareholder Yield vs. FCF Yield

| Entity | Dividend Yield | Net Buyback Yield | Total Shareholder Yield | FCF Yield | FCF ≥ TSY? | Classification |
|--------|--------------|-----------------|----------------------|---------|-----------|---------------|
| **Walmart** | ~1.2% | ~0.5% (net of issuance) | ~1.7% | ~1.9% | ✅ Yes | **Organically funded** |
| **Costco** | ~0.5% | ~0.2% | ~0.7% | ~1.0% | ✅ Yes | **Organically funded** |
| **Target** | ~3.2% | ~0.7% | ~3.9% | ~3.5% | ❌ No (slight) | **Leverage-leaning** |
| **Dollar General** | ~3.0% | 0% (no buybacks FY24) | ~3.0% | ~5.5% | ✅ Yes | **Organically funded** |
| **TJX** | ~1.4% | ~2.0% | ~3.4% | ~4.0% | ✅ Yes | **Organically funded** |
| **Pepco Group** | ~2.0% | 0% | ~2.0% | N/A (net loss) | ❌ No | **Leverage-funded** (inaugural dividend; net loss due to impairment) |
| **Aldi Süd** | N/A (private) | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | Private — sponsor distributions to family foundations |
| **Action** | N/A (private) | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | Private — 3i received ~€500M+ in dividends FY2024 |

**Detailed analysis:**

- **Walmart**: FCF of $12.7B on ~$670B market cap = ~1.9% FCF yield. Dividends (~$8B) + net buybacks (~$3B) = ~$11B = ~1.7% TSY. FCF comfortably covers both.
- **Costco**: FY24 FCF = $6.6B ($11.3B op cash - $4.7B capex) on ~$410B cap = 1.6%. But dividends were $9.0B (including a large special dividend). Normalizing: regular dividends ~$1.3B + buybacks ~$0.7B = ~$2.0B = 0.5% TSY. FCF covers regular distributions.
- **Target**: FY24 FCF = $4.5B ($7.4B op cash - $2.9B capex) = 6.4% FCF yield on lower market cap. But dividends $2.0B + buybacks $1.0B = $3.0B = 4.3% TSY on $70B cap. FCF yield (3.5% on current cap) nearly covers TSY (3.9%); slight gap suggests some leverage funding.
- **Dollar General**: FY24 FCF = $1.7B ($3.0B op cash - $1.3B capex) on $26B cap = 6.5% FCF yield. Dividends ~$0.5B + no buybacks = 2.0% TSY. Very well covered.
- **TJX**: FY25 FCF = ~$5.4B on $137B cap = 3.9% FCF yield. Dividends ~$1.6B + buybacks ~$2.7B = $4.3B = 3.1% TSY. Well covered.
- **Pepco**: FY24 underlying PAT €179M, but reported net loss (€662M) due to €775M non-cash impairment. Inaugural dividend of 6.2 euro cents/share (~€36M) = ~2% yield. Not covered by reported earnings — classified as leverage-funded.
- **Aldi Süd**: Private; no public dividend data. Presumed family foundation distributions from retained earnings.
- **Action**: Private; 3i Group received ~€500M in dividends in FY2024. Action's strong FCF (high EBITDA, moderate capex) organically funds these distributions.

**Capital return program summary:**
- **Organically funded** (FCF yield ≥ TSY): Walmart, Costco, Dollar General, TJX
- **Leverage-funded / borderline** (FCF yield < TSY): Target (slight gap), Pepco (net loss)
- **Private / not applicable**: Aldi Süd, Action (but both generate strong FCF supporting distributions)

**Sources:**
- Walmart FY25 FCF $12.7B — [Walmart 8-K](https://stock.walmart.com/sec-filings/all-sec-filings/content/0000104169-25-000010/earningsreleasefy25q4.htm)
- Costco FY24 FCF calculation ($11.3B op cash - $4.7B capex) — [Costco IR](https://investor.costco.com/news/news-details/2024/Costco-Wholesale-Corporation-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2024-Operating-Results/default.aspx)
- Target FY24 cash flows — [Target earnings release](https://corporate.target.com/press/release/2025/03/target-corporation-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-earnings)
- Dollar General FY24 — [BusinessWire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250311609803/en/Dollar-General-Corporation-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2024-Results)
- TJX FY25 — [TJX 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/109198/000010919825000010/tjx-20250201.htm)
- Pepco inaugural dividend 6.2 euro cents/share — [Pepco PDF](https://www.pepcogroup.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/PCO-FY-2024-Prelim-Results-vFF.pdf)
- 3i Group Action dividends — [3i Group AR24](https://www.3i-usinvestors.com/media/nnrkjwke/annual_report_and_accounts_2024.pdf)

---

## Summary of Rankings and Cross-Cutting Observations

| Dimension | Leader | Notable |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| **Non-Merchandise Revenue Share** | Costco (1.9%) | Target (1.6%) close second; membership/ads as profit engine |
| **Store Growth (3yr CAGR)** | Action (15.2%) | Pepco (13.8%); both in European discount expansion mode |
| **Comp Quality (Traffic-led)** | Walmart (+3.6% traffic) | Target (+1.4% traffic despite flat comps); Action (volume-driven 10.3% LFL) |
| **GAAP Operating Margin** | TJX (8.7%) | Costco drops to 1.8% normalized (membership stripped) |
| **Digital Penetration** | Target (19.6%) | Walmart (16%) fastest growing toward 25% |
| **Revenue per Employee** | Costco ($764K) | Aldi Süd ($456K) best among hard discount |
| **EV per Store** | Costco ($456M/store) | Outlier vs. all peers; membership model premium |
| **FCF Coverage** | Dollar General (6.5% FCF yield) | Target (~3.5% FCF yield barely covers ~3.9% TSY) |

Q1.rationale: Several figures use prior fiscal years and weak page-level sourcing, but Walmart/Costco/Pepco/Action are directionally close. TJX is materially penalized for inventing a stand-alone credit-card/royalty line, and Aldi lacks the required Bundesanzeiger/LZ inference method.

Q2.rationale: Most public-company total store counts are roughly close, but banner-level engines/drags are often incomplete or wrong. Aldi and Action lack acceptable private/sponsor-derived methodology and have materially inflated growth.

Q3.rationale: This section has major sign and disclosure errors: Target comp sign is wrong, DG traffic sign is wrong, Costco/TJX disclosed traffic information is missed, and private/ND handling is poor. Revenue bridges generally do not reconcile to the required one-decimal components.

Q4.rationale: Walmart, Costco, and Target are directionally close on normalized margins, but the answer wrongly identifies Target as the largest rank-shifter and misses required IFRS-to-US-GAAP EBIT reconciliations. TJX and Action use materially wrong operating-margin bases.

Q5.rationale: Digital penetration is frequently based on stale or reconstructed figures without the required T-2 anchors and CAGR derivations. Costco is materially overstated, while private-entity inference bases are mostly absent.

Q6.rationale: Revenue/headcount is often directionally close, but FTE handling is weak: Costco’s disclosed FT/PT split is ignored, Pepco’s FTE is confused with headcount, and several FTE estimates lack the required method. Private-entity sourcing is also too thin.

Q7.rationale: Some EV/store outputs are near the reference, but market-date discipline and net-debt builds are weak. Action is mis-bucketed, Aldi is not correctly identified as the hard-discount bucket outlier, and several private valuation methods are under-supported.

Q8.rationale: Capital-return yields are often stale or materially off, with Target and Pepco misclassified. Private entities are acknowledged but lack the required quantitative substitute methodology.

**Key Findings:**
1. **TJX** is the undisputed profitability leader (11.5% operating margin) with the most efficient off-price model.
2. **Costco's** membership dependency is structurally unique: stripping membership fees drops its margin from 3.8% to 1.9% — the largest rank shift of any entity.
3. **Action** is the fastest grower (13.5% store CAGR, 21.7% revenue growth) — the 3i growth engine.
4. **Costco** has the highest EV/store ($429M), driven by the membership moat and warehouse revenue density.
5. **Target** is the only entity with negative comp sales (-2.6%), and its digital growth has plateaued near 20%.
6. **Walmart's** advertising business ($6.4B) is its fastest-growing non-merchandise stream but still only ~1% of total revenue.

Q1.rationale: Several public-company revenue totals are directionally close, but the candidate uses mixed fiscal years, weak citations, wrong Target/Pepco/Aldi figures, and misses key ND/FX/source handling. Dependency ranking is wrong, especially placing Target ahead of Costco.

Q2.rationale: Store counts are partly close for Costco/Target/Action, but several series use wrong anchors or fiscal years and banner decomposition is often thin or wrong. Pepco is materially wrong due to disposal/exclusion treatment and store-count collapse.

Q3.rationale: The candidate frequently uses FY25/other-period figures inconsistent with the reference, reverses key traffic/ticket signs for Target and Dollar General, and provides weak or missing bridges. TJX is the only materially correct traffic-led comp treatment.

Q4.rationale: Walmart and Costco are directionally close and Costco is correctly identified as a major rank shifter, but many margins use wrong fiscal-year figures or even EBITDA/pretax metrics. IFRS-to-GAAP treatment for Pepco/Action is substantively wrong or absent.

Q5.rationale: The answer captures some high-level digital materiality calls, but lacks proper T-2 anchors, derivations, and source tiers. Aldi Süd is wrong by treating Instacart as a material Süd-wide digital base and projecting FY2029.

Q6.rationale: Walmart and Target are directionally acceptable, but FTE methods are mostly unstated or wrong and disclosed FTE/FT-PT splits for Costco and Pepco are mishandled. Aldi Süd and Pepco figures are materially incorrect.

Q7.rationale: Target and Costco are roughly in range, but the common market-data date is missing and several EV builds are materially wrong. Private-entity valuation methods are weak, Action is mis-bucketed, and the outlier analysis does not follow the required bucket-median logic.

Q8.rationale: Costco is directionally funded by FCF, but most listed yields use wrong market caps, dividend/buyback assumptions, or stale data. Pepco is incorrectly shown with active dividend/buyback yield, and private-company substitutes lack the required quantified methodology.

## Q4. Operating Margin — GAAP vs. Normalized Merchandise-Only

### Methodology
**GAAP operating margin** = Operating income / Total revenue

**Normalized merchandise-only margin** strips: (i) membership/subscription fees (treated as ~100% margin), (ii) credit/financial income, (iii) advertising/media income — each added back as zero-cost revenue. Formula:

> Normalized merchandise OpInc = GAAP Operating Income − (Other Revenue × assumed 100% margin) + Other Revenue  
> Normalized merch. margin = Normalized merch. OpInc / Merchandise Sales  
> *(Equivalently: Normalized merch. margin = (GAAP OpInc − Non-merchandise income) / Merchandise revenue)*

### Outlier: **Costco vs. the Mass Merchant Bucket**

Costco's EV/Store ($389.6M) is **4.5× the mass merchant median ($87.3M)** and **14× the dollar/hard-discount median ($2.0M)**.

Within the dollar/hard-discount bucket, **Dollar General ($1.8M) vs. bucket median ($2.0M)**: DG trades at a **10% discount to its bucket median** — not a dramatic outlier.

The **true structural outlier is Action vs. the hard-discount bucket**: Action at **$2.2M/store** is **10% above the hard-discount median ($2.0M)**, despite being the fastest-growing, highest-LFL (+10.3%) business in the group.

### Structural Driver of the Costco Outlier

Costco's $389.6M EV/warehouse vs. Walmart's $133.4M per-store EV reflects fundamentally different business models:

| Driver | Walmart | Costco |
|---|---|---|
| **Revenue/Store** | ~$61M (mass merchant) | ~$280M (warehouse club) |
| **Gross Margin** | ~24-25% | ~12-13% |
| **Operating Income/Store** | ~$2.6M | ~$10.4M |
| **Membership Moat** | None | $4.8B recurring, high renewal (90%+) |
| **Capital Intensity** | Moderate (lease-heavy) | High (owned real estate) |
| **Geographic Diversification** | Global | US-centric (15 countries) |

Costco's per-store EV premium is justified by: (i) **4.6× higher revenue per warehouse** ($280M vs. $61M), (ii) **near-monopoly in membership warehouse** (only major US competitor is Sam's Club), (iii) **high membership renewal rates** (~90%) creating predictable recurring income, and (iv) **ownership of real estate** at most locations. The implied $389.6M/store vs. ~$30-50M replacement cost indicates significant goodwill/membership franchise value embedded in the EV.

---

## Q8. Total Shareholder Yield vs. FCF Yield

### Listed Entities

| Entity | Market Cap (FY24 ref.) | Dividend Yield | Buyback Yield | **Shareholder Yield** | FCF ($B) | **FCF Yield** | **Classification** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Costco** | ~$355B | 0.5% (1) | 0.2% | **~0.7%** | ~$6.6B | **1.9%** | **Organically funded** |
| **Target** | ~$63B | ~3.4% (2) | ~0% | **~3.4%** | ~$4.3B | **6.8%** | **Organically funded** |
| **TJX** | ~$131B | ~1.2% (3) | ~1.3% (4) | **~2.5%** | ~$4.0B | **3.1%** | **Organically funded** |
| **Walmart** | ~$500B (5) | 0.7% | ~1.6% (6) | **~2.3%** | ~$25.6B | **5.1%** | **Organically funded** |
| **Dollar General** | ~$29B | ~3.1% (7) | 0.0% (8) | **~3.1%** | ~$1.9B | **6.6%** | **Organically funded** |
| **Pepco Group** | ~$4.0B | ~1.3% (9) | ~0% | **~1.3%** | €168M | **~4.2%** | **Organically funded** |

**Sources and Calculations:**
1. Costco: Quarterly dividend $0.15/share × 4 = $0.60/year + special $15.00/share dividend (Jan 2024). Regular annual dividend ~$0.60 × 443M shares = ~$265M ≈ 0.07% on $355B market cap. Annualized dividend yield ~0.5%. Buyback $700M / $355B ≈ 0.2%. FCF = $11,339M − $4,710M = $6,629M (FY2024).
2. Target: Dividend yield ~3-3.5% (~$3.72/share annualized / ~$148 share price ≈ 2.5%; updated). TTM FY2024 yield ~3.1-3.4%.
3. TJX: Dividend $1.72/share (FY2024 annualized) / ~$115 ≈ 1.5%; FY2024 buyback $1.7B / $131B ≈ 1.3%.
4. TJX: FY2024 buyback ~$1.7B; total returned $4.1B (buyback + dividend). FY2024 FCF ≈ $4.0B.
5. Walmart: Market cap at $168/share × 8.1B shares ≈ $1,361B (FY2024). At ~$62/share (Jan 2025): $62 × 8.0B ≈ $496B. Using Jan 2024 price for FY2024 analysis.
6. Walmart: FY2024 share repurchase $20B authorized; actual FY2024 buybacks ~$7.5B / $500B ≈ 1.5%; FY2024 dividend yield $0.76/$168 ≈ 0.45%. Total ~2.0%.
7. Dollar General: Dividend $2.36/share (FY2024 annualized) / ~$136 ≈ 1.7% (FY2024). FY2025 dividend yield ~3.1%.
8. Dollar General: "No repurchases during fiscal 2024" per 10-K. Source: DG 10-K FY2024.
9. Pepco: Inaugural dividend announced FY2024; DPS €6.2 cents. Share price ~28 PLN (~€6.4 / ~$7). Yield ≈ 0.9% (in PLN). USD-adjusted ~1.3%.

**Classification Analysis:**

| Entity | FCF Yield vs. Shareholder Yield | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| **Walmart** | 5.1% FCF vs. ~2.3% SY | Organically funded (FCF > SY) |
| **Target** | 6.8% FCF vs. ~3.4% SY | **Organically funded** |

| **Pepco** | ~4.2% FCF vs. ~1.3% SY | **Organically funded** |

**Note:** All listed entities show organically funded capital-return programs (FCF yield > shareholder yield), meaning each generates sufficient free cash flow to cover dividends and buybacks without relying on debt-financed distributions. Walmart's large gap (5.1% FCF vs. 2.3% SY = 2.8pp excess) indicates significant FCF headroom for accelerated buybacks or special dividends.

**Special Dividend Impact on Costco:** Costco's January 2024 special dividend of $15/share (~$6.65B total) distorts the FY2024 shareholder yield calculation. On a recurring basis (excluding the special), Costco's regular annual dividend is ~$0.60/share (0.07%) plus buybacks (0.2%), for a recurring SY of ~0.27% — still organically covered by 1.9% FCF yield.

### Tier-2 Private Entities

| Entity | Capital Return Activity | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| **Aldi Süd** | No public distributions (privately held by heirs of Theo Albrecht Sr.); no disclosed dividend or buyback policy | N/A (private) |

Most recent distribution: 3i sold ~5% stake in 2021 at ~£1.5B valuation; partial exit via dividend recap (3i used Action dividends to fund distributions to LPs). 3i AR24 shows Action generating strong EBITDA (~$700M est.) used for debt repayment and distributions. | **Sponsor distributions via dividend recap; leverage-funded at sponsor level** |

| Dimension | #1 Performer | Notable Finding |

| **Q1 Non-Merch. Dependency** | **Costco** (1.9%) | All others <1% merchandise revenue |

| **Q7 EV/Store Outlier** | **Costco** ($389.6M) | 4.5× mass merchant median; warehouse club model justifies premium |
| **Q8 Organic Funding** | **All listed** | All 6 listed entities organically funded (FCF > SY) |

Q1.rationale: Mostly directionally identifies merchandise-heavy models and Costco membership dependence, but uses stale fiscal years, weak/generic citations, and misses key decompositions such as Target Roundel/TD and TJX rental income. Private-entity source handling is weak, especially Aldi Süd.

Q2.rationale: Store-count series are often stale, incomplete, or materially wrong, and Costco is omitted entirely. Banner-level engine/drag analysis is partial and several net-add/CAGR calculations are far from the reference.

Q3.rationale: The answer frequently uses wrong fiscal years and incorrect comp/traffic/ticket signs, including Target and Dollar General. Required revenue bridges are mostly incomplete or non-reconciling, and several non-disclosed traffic splits are mishandled.

Q5.rationale: The answer captures that Walmart/Target lead and hard discounters are mostly non-digital, but uses stale anchors and wrong Costco/Walmart penetration figures. CAGR and TT25 derivations are often absent or materially off, with weak inference bases for private entities.

Q6.rationale: Revenue-per-headcount is sometimes directionally close, but FTE adjustments are missing, estimated without method, or wrong for key disclosed cases like Costco and Pepco. Several employee and store bases rely on weak non-primary sources.

Q7.rationale: Some listed EV/store values are directionally close, but the market-date basis is inconsistent and Walmart, Aldi Süd, and Action are materially wrong. Bucket medians and the outlier analysis are distorted by mis-bucketing and stale private valuations.

Q8.rationale: Costco is handled well, including special-dividend treatment, but most other yield figures use stale market caps or wrong buyback/FCF inputs. Pepco is incorrectly shown with an active dividend, and private-entity substitutes are underdeveloped.

**Normalization methodology**
- **Costco:** Membership fees ($4.8bn) treated as 100% margin. Merch-only revenue = $249.6bn. Merch-only operating income = $9.285bn - $4.828bn = $4.457bn → **1.80%**.
- **Target:** Advertising ($0.649bn) + credit-card profit sharing ($0.576bn) = $1.225bn treated as 100% margin. Merch-only revenue = $104.8bn. Merch-only operating income = $5.566bn - $1.225bn = $4.341bn → **4.14%**.

**Entity whose rank shifts most:** **Costco**. It falls from a mid-tier GAAP margin (~3.65%) to the lowest merchandise-only margin (~1.80%) once the high-margin membership fee is stripped out, reflecting the warehouse-club model where merchandise is sold at near-cost.

**IFRS-to-GAAP reconciliation note:** Pepco, Aldi Süd, and Action report under IFRS (or Dutch GAAP/Local GAAP for Action).
